field_rule:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1239) — Under the Flora name Andropogon glomeratus, look for many short flowering branches crowded into a broom-shaped cluster. The Flora gives branch lengths of 1.5–3 cm.

Bushy bluestem is a tufted perennial with erect culms often about 75–150 cm in Kew GrassBase. Numerous crowded short flowering units make a broad, cottony terminal brush, unlike broomsedge's more separated spathe-held units. Texas Uvalde whole-clump and USGS flowering photographs show this gross architecture; a white head alone is not definitive.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas pp.162–163 under Andropogon glomeratus
head.reference: Crowded many-branched broom-like inflorescences clustered near culm tip; short 1.5–3 cm branches. Current head is source-checked, though accepted Anatherum taxonomy is newer.

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the crowded raceme pairs through their spathes
diagnostic_checks.check: The bushy cluster is a compound group of short hairy paired racemes, typically about 1.5–3 cm, tightly crowded near the top; each pair has sessile fertile spikelets and often reduced pedicelled companions.
diagnostic_checks.compare: broomsedge's more separate spathe-held flower units and the narrow-spathed A. tenuispatheum
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published morphology; exact image-to-character QA pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase under Andropogon glomeratus

diagnostic_checks.look: Use a vegetative check when heads are missing
diagnostic_checks.check: Regional Hill Country treatment reports compressed, keeled leaf sheaths broader than the blades, and a membranous, marginally ciliate ligule about 1–2 mm. This does not alone identify the species.
diagnostic_checks.compare: broomsedge has lower compressed sheaths but upper sheaths more rounded
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Regionally sourced; not sufficient alone
diagnostic_checks.source: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015, p.34

diagnostic_review.note: Measurements are published source descriptions, not verified dimensions on local photographed specimens; do not certify a field ID using head outline alone.

field_rule:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1243) — Compare the main cane and its full flowering head. The Flora describes usually unbranched canes 2–6 m tall and panicles 30–60 cm long.

The locally archived Forest & Kim Starr Maui stand (panel 0) and Duarte Frade roadside stand (panel 1) show actual tall cane-like culms and long broad clasping leaves. Harry Rose's true attached flowering panicle (panel 4) shows the complete many-branched head. Recognize the large rhizomatous reed, but do not claim any ONE photo proves root-to-head linkage or Texas provenance. A permitted disturbed Texas specimen with roots/canes/head in on
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 167
head.reference: Giant reed panicle 30–60 cm on cane-like rhizomatous plant. Rachilla internodes nearly glabrous while lemmas are hairy, opposite relative placement to Phragmites.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 167
habit.reference: Perennial rhizomatous reed, typically very tall.

hair_placement.source: Invasive Plant Science and Management 2023, comparative Arundo donax biology
hair_placement.reference: Arundo lemma densely hairy on lower portion; rachilla between florets nearly glabrous, contrasting Phragmites lemmas mostly glabrous and rachilla densely hairy.

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare a real hollow cane, wide blade base and flowering head
diagnostic_checks.check: Giant reed has thick cane-like culms often 3–10 m, broad leaves with a distinct tan/brown wedge or auricle-like lobe at their sheath junction, and upright plume panicles commonly 30–60 cm. These clues alone are NOT enough in a young nonflowering stand.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Common reed (*Phragmites*) often has thinner stems, blades narrowing more gradually at the base, and an often drooping head; both vary.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA + current peer-reviewed field comparison; same-plant shoot and collar photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Arundo donax

diagnostic_checks.look: Locate HAIRS on the LEMMA instead of the rachilla joint
diagnostic_checks.check: In mature Arundo spikelets (~10–15 mm, usually 2–5 florets), the rachilla segments BETWEEN florets are basically GLABROUS, whereas each LEMMA bears long ~4–9 mm silky hairs low on its back and two little teeth around a short terminal awn.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Phragmites reverses the major hair location: long silky RACHILLA INTERNODE hairs, while mature lemmas are mostly glabrous and long-tapered.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Peer-reviewed 2023 comparison and UT Williamson County specimen; exact same-floret dissection pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Biology of Invasive Plants — Arundo versus Phragmites

diagnostic_checks.look: Check ciliate membrane and true underground solid rhizome
diagnostic_checks.check: Arundo has a short thin membranous ligule (roughly 0.4–1.5 mm depending treatment), glumes usually long enough to nearly enclose florets, and heavy solid-scaled rhizomes below the canes. A rhizome cross-section, if ever legally sampled, differs from Phragmites' hollow-centered rhizome.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Phragmites also rhizomatous and ciliate-ligulate; don't recommend digging or cutting for ID in a managed protected riparian stand.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Published source morphology; comparisons can use authorized archive vouchers, no new wild disturbance required
diagnostic_checks.source: Arundo field comparison — Invasive Plant Science and Management

diagnostic_review.note: Source-linked botanical comparisons complete for first checklist pass only; photo parts, exact lineage where relevant and Hays field specimens not certified. Endangered Zizania strictly observe without disturbance.

field_rule:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1244) — Count florets within one intact spikelet. The Flora key gives usually three or four.

Begin with the TWO archived Texas in-situ Avena fatua photos (panels 4–5): trace each open, often nodding, branched panicle to the pendent spikelets. Panel 0 adds an older source-identified flowering view. None exposes connected roots or proves the mature floret callus. A 7–40 cm panicle and 2–3-flowered large spikelets are published traits, not independently measured from these photographs. Contrast the unbranched spikes of Hordeum and Secale.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.168
head.reference: Open flowering head with large hanging multi-flowered spikelets (typically 3–4 florets); awn often geniculate ~2.5–4 cm.

floral_count.source: Flora of North America Avena fatua; older Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas
floral_count.reference: FNA: 2, sometimes 3, florets in a spikelet, 18–32 mm. Older North Central Texas flora suggests usually 3–4; treat as source conflict to verify with local specimen, not a definitive cut-off.

diagnostic_checks.look: Count florets inside ONE hanging spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: Flora of North America gives usually 2, sometimes 3, florets in each large 18–32 mm hanging wild-oat spikelet. The older North Central Texas regional flora indicates usually 3–4; preserve that discrepancy rather than forcing a count. Also inspect the open branched panicle, not just a detached lemma.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Bromus often has 6–20 florets, rye and barley flowering units are attached directly along a spike
diagnostic_checks.certainty: CONFLICTING floret counts: FNA 2(3), older regional flora 3–4; verify attached Texas specimens
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Avena fatua, with regional-flora discrepancy noted

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect a long bent lemma awn at maturity
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA gives a 23–42 mm awn arising from the middle THIRD of a 14–22 mm lemma, usually twisted and bent; this dorsal insertion differs from the terminal awns of Aristida and the subapical awns of many Bromus.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Threeawns have THREE awns on one lemma; brome awns are typically straight to divergent
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Regional-flora sourced; section not independently photo-certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Avena fatua

diagnostic_review.note: Regional or FNA/GrassBase measurements; not measured on authenticated Hays County specimens or verified in current key photos.

Start with Matt Lavin's genuine silvery panicle (panel 0), then see Austin flowering habitat (panel 7). A detached fuzzy head alone is insufficient.

diagnostic_checks.look: Confirm a TRUE membrane at the collar
diagnostic_checks.check: Bromus has a membrane ligule, even if hair fringes occur at adjacent collar or sheath positions; B. pubescens accounts describe about 2–4 mm in a Texas study. Look inside the blade–sheath junction.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Annual bromes also have membranes, so this confirms group but not species
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Texas PRC regional source; not species-separating alone
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin Plant Resources Center, Vascular Plants of Williamson County — Bromus pubescens

photos.label: Common Sandbur — spines around the outside of the bur
photos.creator: Harry Rose / Macleay Grass Man

field_rule: The actual spine-bearing dispersal unit is a cupule of fused bristles enclosing true spikelets. Identify regional sandbur to species from mature measured bristle/base characters, dissected florets, and a confirmed specimen—not photographs of prickles alone.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.178
head.reference: Spiny bur has retrorsely barbed spines; distinguish fused bristle cupule from separate persistent Setaria bristles.

diagnostic_checks.look: Open a mature fused burr carefully
diagnostic_checks.check: The spiny unit is a cup-shaped INVOLUCRE of fused bristles around roughly 2–4 actual spikelets, not a seed with many lemma awns. Kew describes a burr 5.5–10.2 mm long and flattened reflex-barbed spines.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Setaria has individual, unfused bristles that persist below spikelets when the spikelets fall
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase-backed; avoid handling barehanded; fused cup macro pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Cenchrus spinifex

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the collar and break-off scar
diagnostic_checks.check: The ligule is a fringe of hairs (~0.5–1.5 mm); burr clusters break away along the axis, leaving scars. Count the actual spikelets inside a burr with magnification, and retain species-level caution if the burr is immature.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Other sandbur species can also have fused spiny involucres; species requires correctly measured mature burr
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase-backed; species-level macro pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Cenchrus spinifex
